name: Plain weave
summary: Each yarn alternates over and under its neighbors in the smallest woven repeat.
construction: Every warp passes over one weft and under the next. Adjacent warps reverse that sequence, giving a repeat of two ends and two picks.
recognize: Look closely for a regular one-over, one-under grid with no long floats.
distinguish: Plain describes the interlacing, not a plain color: the same structure can carry checks, stripes or printed flowers.

name: Basket weave
summary: Groups of yarns act together to make a larger version of plain weave.
construction: Two or more neighboring warps pass together over and under groups of wefts. The example is a balanced 2 by 2 basket; unequal groupings are also possible.
recognize: Look for small woven blocks, with neighboring yarns following the same path.
distinguish: The grouped crossings separate basket weave from a single-thread plain weave; Oxford is a familiar uneven variation.

name: Rib weave
summary: An extended plain-weave structure emphasizes ribs in one direction.
construction: Plain weave can be extended along warp or weft while retaining alternating interlacing groups. Yarn thickness and close spacing determine how strongly the ribs stand out.
recognize: Look for repeated lengthwise or crosswise ridges rather than a diagonal twill line.
distinguish: Woven rib is structurally different from knitted rib, and a ribbed appearance alone does not identify one exact weave.

references.title: KSRCT: Fabric Structure and Design, plain-weave derivatives

name: Twill
summary: Staggered yarn floats create the diagonal lines shared by a large family of weaves.
construction: Interlacing positions move along by a regular step from one pick to the next. The illustrated 2/2 repeat is one member of a family that also includes 2/1 and 3/1 twills.
recognize: Trace the diagonal ribs across the surface; their slope and prominence depend on the construction.
distinguish: Twill is an interlacing family. Denim and gabardine are fabrics that use it, while houndstooth adds a color arrangement.

name: 2/1 twill
summary: A three-thread twill repeat places more warp than weft on the illustrated face.
construction: Each warp goes over two picks and under one. Shifting the crossing by one yarn on successive picks produces a three-end, three-pick diagonal repeat.
recognize: The visible floats are shorter than those in 3/1 twill, with a contrasting reverse.
distinguish: The numbers describe warp-over and warp-under counts, not yarn colors or the number of plies.

name: 2/2 twill
summary: A balanced four-thread twill shows equal warp and weft interlacing counts.
construction: Each warp floats over two picks and under two. The crossings shift by one position on each pick to form the diagonal.
recognize: Both sides have the same interlacing balance, although yarn color, density and finishing may make them look different.
distinguish: Balanced interlacing does not guarantee identical yarn sizes or equal thread density.

name: 3/1 twill
summary: A four-thread twill puts three warp crossings on the face for every one below.
construction: Each warp passes over three successive picks and under one. The long warp floats create a face that can emphasize a colored warp over a lighter weft.
recognize: Look for a strong diagonal and a face that differs markedly from the reverse when warp and weft colors contrast.
distinguish: It shares a four-thread repeat with 2/2 twill but has unequal face and back interlacing counts.

name: Herringbone
summary: Alternating bands of opposing twill direction create a broken zigzag.
construction: A group of right-slanting twills is followed by a group that slants left. This teaching repeat reverses a 2/2 twill with an offset at the meeting line rather than a continuous point.
recognize: Look for narrow columns of slanting ribs that reverse direction with a visible break.
distinguish: Herringbone describes this twill arrangement; houndstooth is a tooth-shaped color-and-weave pattern. A printed zigzag can imitate the look without this structure.

references.title: CottonWorks: Textile Weaving, herringbone and chevron diagrams

name: Broken twill
summary: A family of twills interrupts the continuous diagonal through a change in sequence or direction.
construction: Warp or weft ordering is altered so that the twill line no longer runs uninterrupted. Herringbone is a recognizable example; other broken repeats need not form the same wide zigzag.
recognize: Look for interrupted, reversed or staggered diagonal segments.
distinguish: Broken twill is a broader construction description than herringbone, so the name does not specify one universal draft.

name: Satin
summary: Long floats and separated binding points produce a smooth woven face.
construction: The binding points are distributed so neighboring points do not create the continuous diagonal of a simple twill. This example is a five-end warp-faced satin, with one binding point per row and column.
recognize: Look for extended smooth yarn surfaces and a face that catches light differently from the back.
distinguish: Satin names a weave as well as fabrics made with it; it does not by itself mean silk.

name: Sateen
summary: A satin-structured fabric, commonly made with cotton yarns, presents a smooth face.
construction: Long floats dominate the face, with scattered binding points. The illustrated five-end weft-faced repeat is a common teaching example; trade usage of satin and sateen varies.
recognize: The surface is smoother and often more lustrous than a comparable plain-weave cotton.
distinguish: Sateen is not a fiber or a thread-count grade, and the name alone does not guarantee one float direction.

name: Dobby weaving
summary: A shaft-control system produces small repeating woven figures and textures.
construction: A dobby selects combinations of shafts, moving the warp ends threaded through those shafts together. Many different interlacings can be woven this way, so there is no single dobby draft.
recognize: Small dots, diamonds or other repeating geometry are common, but appearance alone cannot prove the loom type.
distinguish: Dobby identifies pattern control and a fabric family, not a fourth basic weave alongside plain, twill and satin.

name: Jacquard weaving
summary: Individual warp control allows elaborate woven designs with large or detailed repeats.
construction: A Jacquard mechanism selects warp ends with more individual control than ordinary shaft grouping. It can combine different binding systems and colors within one design.
recognize: Look for a design formed by the yarn interlacings, often visible in altered form on the reverse.
distinguish: Jacquard describes a method of pattern control. Damask, brocade and other structures may be made with that method.

name: Leno weave
summary: Paired warp yarns cross around one another to secure an open woven structure.
construction: Warp partners move across each other around the weft rather than remaining in fixed parallel columns. This crossing helps hold the open mesh together.
recognize: Under magnification, follow the twisting warp pairs around the weft crossings.
distinguish: A normal binary over-under grid cannot show the lateral warp crossings. The illustration is only a visual cue, not a leno draft.

name: Mock leno
summary: Grouped interlacings produce open areas that resemble leno without crossing warp pairs.
construction: Yarn groups and floats encourage threads to gather into clusters around openings. Thread spacing and finishing matter as well as the lifting sequence.
recognize: Look for a lacy grid whose warp threads remain in their original order.
distinguish: Mock leno imitates an open appearance; true leno physically crosses neighboring warp yarns.

references.title: Thayercraft: Leno and mock leno, microscopic examples
MemphisWeaver: Leno vs. Mock Leno, maker demonstration

name: Waffle weave
summary: A cellular woven texture forms recessed centers bounded by raised ridges.
construction: Arranged warp and weft floats draw into a three-dimensional surface when the cloth relaxes and is finished. Different repeats change the size and depth of the cells.
recognize: Look for repeated square or diamond-like hollows, with raised borders you can feel.
distinguish: Waffle describes a surface also found in knits; check for crossing yarns before identifying a woven waffle.

references.title: Ashford: The Wheel 35, Double Heddle Waffle Weave

name: Woven piqué
summary: Raised woven ribs or small geometric textures give piqué a patterned surface.
construction: The texture is built into the cloth during weaving. Commercial examples include small birdseye-like formal shirting and more pronounced patterned constructions.
recognize: Look for a stable woven ground with raised dots, cords or small geometric relief.
distinguish: The piqué used for many polo shirts is knitted. Woven piqué is a separate construction family, not proof of a single repeat.

references.title: Beautiful People: Thomas Mason piqué construction and shirt details

name: Birdseye weave
summary: Small repeated eye-like figures give several woven constructions their birdseye name.
construction: Interlacing and sometimes contrasting yarn colors outline tiny spots or lozenges. The name covers related visual effects rather than one universally fixed draft.
recognize: Look for regularly spaced small eyes or dots, often clearer close up than at a distance.
distinguish: A birdseye effect can arise from structure or color-and-weave interaction; it is not automatically a printed polka dot.

references.title: KSRCT: Fabric Structure and Design, birdseye and spot effects
University of Illinois Extension: textile identification, birdseye weave

name: Diamond twill
summary: Twill directions reverse along both axes to outline woven diamonds.
construction: A pointed sequence across the warp is combined with a reversing sequence of picks. The resulting repeat turns the diagonal lines into lozenges rather than an uninterrupted diagonal.
recognize: Trace the diagonal ribs to see whether they meet around a repeating diamond.
distinguish: A diamond motif can be printed or knitted too; diamond twill specifically describes a woven interlacing.

name: Double cloth
summary: Two layers are woven together and may be joined or exchanged to form a design.
construction: Each layer has its own warp and weft system in a typical double-cloth construction. Layers can exchange positions at selected places, making reversible patterns or pockets between them.
recognize: Examine both faces and an unfinished edge for two connected layers.
distinguish: Double cloth is made during weaving; two separate fabrics glued or sewn together are not automatically double cloth.

references.title: Cooper Hewitt: Color Decoded, double-cloth construction
National Museum of Finland: The mystery of the double cloth

name: Tapestry weaving
summary: Discontinuous colored wefts build a design while covering the warp.
construction: Weft yarns work back and forth within selected areas rather than necessarily spanning the full width. Packing them closely hides the warp and creates blocks of color.
recognize: Look for a weft-dominated face and color areas built into the fabric itself.
distinguish: Needlepoint stitches are worked into an existing ground; tapestry weaving creates the cloth as it creates the image.

name: Damask
summary: Contrasting bindings create a figured woven design that reverses between the two faces.
construction: Classical damask uses one warp and one weft, changing the interlacing between figure and ground. Satin-based examples use different float directions to change how light reflects.
recognize: Tilt the fabric and turn it over: the figure and ground often exchange light and dark appearances.
distinguish: Damask forms contrast through its binding systems; brocade commonly adds supplementary pattern yarns.

references.title: Museo del Traje: Silk damask cloth

name: Brocade
summary: Additional pattern yarns create figured decoration over a woven ground.
construction: Supplementary yarns form decorative areas while the underlying fabric supplies its ground structure. These patterning yarns can differ in color or material, including metallic threads.
recognize: Look for figured areas that appear raised or distinct from the background and inspect the extra yarns on the reverse.
distinguish: Brocade is a woven fabric family, not simply any floral pattern or any fabric made on a Jacquard loom.

references.title: Museum of Fine Arts CAMEO: Brocade
MFA CAMEO: Silk textile with supplementary brocade weft

name: Matelassé
summary: A sculpted woven surface creates a quilted-looking pattern.
construction: Patterned weaving creates raised and recessed areas within the fabric. Contemporary matelassé bedding is commonly Jacquard-woven and may use a layered construction.
recognize: Look for puffed geometric or floral relief that is woven into the cloth.
distinguish: The quilted appearance does not necessarily mean that separate fabric layers have been stitched around batting.

references.title: Fitzwilliam Museum: Double weave and matelassé

name: Velvet
summary: An extra warp system forms a dense pile above the woven ground.
construction: Pile warp yarns rise from a ground cloth to form loops that may be cut, left intact or combined in patterns. The short upright pile gives the surface its characteristic light response.
recognize: Gently change the pile direction to see the shade change; examine the backing for a woven ground.
distinguish: Woven velvet uses a pile warp, while corduroy forms its characteristic pile from filling floats. A velvet-like appearance alone does not identify the fiber.

references.title: V&A: Project Interwoven, examining velvet pile structure

name: Corduroy
summary: Rows of cut pile make corduroy’s lengthwise ribs, known as wales.
construction: Extra filling floats are woven into the cloth and then cut. The exposed yarn ends form the soft parallel cords above the ground.
recognize: Look for pile ridges separated by channels; wale count describes how many ridges occupy a given width.
distinguish: The cords are cut pile, not knitted rib. Narrow and wide wales are variations within the fabric family.

name: Woven terry
summary: Uncut loops project from a woven ground to create a toweling surface.
construction: A ground warp holds the cloth together while a separately fed pile warp forms loops. The loom controls yarn delivery and beat-up to build the pile.
recognize: Look for intact loops on one or both faces above a woven backing.
distinguish: French terry is commonly knitted; check the backing instead of using the word terry alone to identify construction.

name: Gauze
summary: A lightweight open fabric family provides a sheer, airy surface.
construction: Widely spaced yarns create an open cloth. The name can cover plain-woven versions and fabrics using leno crossings, so the exact construction needs inspection.
recognize: Light passes readily through visible spaces between yarns.
distinguish: Gauze is broader than leno. The fabric name alone does not establish medical suitability or any tested performance.

name: Canvas
summary: A firm, typically heavy plain-woven fabric emphasizes sturdy yarns and close construction.
construction: The basic crossings follow plain weave. Substantial yarns and fabric density give canvas its characteristic body rather than a special diagonal or pile structure.
recognize: Look for a coarse visible grid and a firm hand.
distinguish: Canvas and duck overlap in trade usage; the name does not specify a waterproof coating or one fiber composition.

name: Poplin
summary: A closely woven plain-weave fabric offers a smooth shirting surface, sometimes with a fine crosswise rib.
construction: Single warp and weft yarns alternate in a plain weave. Relative yarn size and spacing can create a subtle rib across the cloth.
recognize: Look for a fine even surface without twill diagonals or grouped basket crossings.
distinguish: Broadcloth can mean poplin-like cotton shirting in some markets, but the term also has other textile meanings.

name: Oxford cloth
summary: A basket-weave shirting groups warp yarns together to create visible texture.
construction: Typically, two warp ends work together over and under each filling yarn. The filling is often heavier than an individual warp end.
recognize: Look for grouped crossings and a slightly grainy basket surface.
distinguish: Oxford is a fabric construction, not a collar style. The illustrated 2 by 1 grouping is not a 2/1 twill.

name: Pinpoint Oxford
summary: A finer Oxford variation retains grouped crossings with a smoother, smaller-scale texture.
construction: It uses the Oxford grouping principle with finer yarns than a coarse casual Oxford. CottonWorks distinguishes pinpoint as using warp and filling yarns of equal size.
recognize: Examine the small basket-like crossings under magnification rather than expecting an obvious dot print.
distinguish: Pinpoint Oxford should not be confused with an arbitrary pinpoint-sized printed dot.

name: Chambray
summary: A colored warp and a lighter filling create a softly mixed color in a plain weave.
construction: The classic cotton version combines dyed warp yarns with white weft yarns. Both directions remain visible through the one-over, one-under crossings.
recognize: Look for a subtle two-color grid, usually with more similar faces than a warp-faced denim.
distinguish: A blue color does not make chambray denim: chambray is plain-woven, while conventional denim is twill.

name: Denim
summary: A twill fabric commonly combines colored warp yarns with pale filling yarns.
construction: Conventional denim is often a 3/1 warp-faced twill, placing more of the dyed warp on the face. Other weights and twill variations exist, including broken twills.
recognize: Look for diagonal ribs and, in classic blue denim, a lighter reverse.
distinguish: Denim identifies a fabric family. Selvedge describes an edge, and raw describes a finishing state; neither is a separate weave.

references.title: CottonWorks: Textile Weaving, denim and 3/1 twill

name: Gabardine
summary: A closely set twill presents fine diagonal ribs and a comparatively smooth reverse.
construction: Dense construction emphasizes a clear twill face, commonly with a steep diagonal. Fiber, yarn and finishing choices vary between wool, cotton and manufactured-fiber versions.
recognize: Look for fine, closely spaced diagonal lines rather than a coarse denim-like surface.
distinguish: The word gabardine does not guarantee rain protection; any water-resistance claim belongs to the particular finished fabric.

references.title: University of Arizona weaving archive: Focus on Fabrics, gabardine

name: Drill
summary: A firm twill fabric is widely used where clothing needs substantial body.
construction: Drill commonly uses a compact 2/1 twill in cotton or manufactured fibers. The illustrated repeat shows that interlacing rather than a particular yarn weight.
recognize: Look for clear diagonal ribs in a sturdy cloth.
distinguish: Drill is a fabric name, not a promise of a specific fiber or measured strength.

references.title: CBSE: Fabric Study, drill construction and uses

name: Seersucker
summary: Alternating puckered and smoother bands give this cloth its recognizable relief.
construction: In woven seersucker, selected warp groups are supplied under different tension or feed conditions. Their unequal take-up builds the puckered surface into the cloth.
recognize: Look for physical puckers that remain when the fabric lies flat, not merely printed stripes.
distinguish: Seersucker is not limited to blue-and-white stripes; a solid-color version can have the same textured construction.

references.title: Proper Cloth: White seersucker fabric example

name: Crepe weave
summary: Irregularly arranged interlacings create a granular surface without an obvious directional line.
construction: Floats and binding points are distributed to suppress the obvious grid or diagonal of basic weaves. Many different repeats can produce this effect.
recognize: Look for a small-scale pebbled texture with no strong continuous rib.
distinguish: Crepe fabric can also gain its texture from highly twisted yarns or finishing; a crepe appearance does not prove crepe interlacing.

name: Percale
summary: A smooth plain-woven fabric is familiar as a crisp style of sheeting.
construction: Warp and weft alternate one over and one under. Yarn choice, density and finishing affect how crisp or soft the finished cloth feels.
recognize: Look for a fine plain-weave grid without the long face floats of sateen.
distinguish: Percale describes a fabric construction and market family, not a cotton variety or an automatic quality ranking.
